newsitem.title: USA: Scientists find proof prostate cancer hereditary. [Corrected 2:29 gmt 22/11]
newsitem.headline: Scientists find proof prostate cancer hereditary. [Corrected 2:29 gmt 22/11]

text.p: Researchers have found the first proof that prostate cancer runs in families, locating a gene that increases the likelihood of developing the disease.

The finding, to be published in Friday's edition of the journal Science, is expected to shed light on how prostate cancer develops and perhaps on how to prevent and treat it, the researchers told a news conference.
About 317,000 men in the United States will be diagnosed with prostate cancer this year.
"We have not yet got the gene in our clutches," said Francis Collins, who heads the National Centre for Human Genome Research in Baltimore. (Deletes reference to Johns Hopkins University).

But he acknowledged the discovery of the prostate cancer gene's location could help scientists develop a test for the estimated 250,000 American men who may have the genetic characteristic that increases susceptibility to the disease.

Under questioning, he declined to say when such a test might be available but pointed to a similar path as that followed in the case of hereditary breast cancer: research into the genetic component of that disease was at about the same point six years ago that prostate cancer is now, he said, and genetic testing for breast cancer is now proceeding.
Harold Varmus, director of the National Institutes of Health, stressed that there should be no immediate change in how prostate cancer is treated.

In the Science article, researchers at the genome centre and Umea University in Sweden reported on a study involving 91 familes in which at least three members suffered from prostate cancer. The gene they discovered, called HPC-1 for hereditary prostate cancer, is situated on the long arm of the chromosome, they said, and alterations to it account for at least a third of familial prostate cancer.
The researchers said testing for genetic susceptibility and for the presence of the HPC-1 gene could lead to early detection and prevent deaths.

In the United States, men stand a one-in-five chance of developing the cancer, the most common among men and the cause of more than 40,000 deaths a year. Researchers suspect that high-fat diets, multiple sex partners and cigarette smoking may heighten the risk, but not conclusively.
Familial or heriditary prostate cancer accounts for about one in 10 cases, the researchers said.

"We know this gene seems to contribute to prostate cancer risk in a number of ethnic backgrounds," said Dr. Jeffrey Trent, head of the laboratory at Johns Hopkins where the gene research was conducted. "There's linkage in Swedish families as well as American families, including African American families."

At the news conference, Trent likened the prostate cancer gene to a serial killer on the loose: the discovery of the gene's neighbourhood and certain similarities among its victims greatly narrows the search for the "killer" even without knowing exactly what it looks like.
Prostate cancer varies widely among ethnic groups with African American men suffering the highest rate in the world, 180 per 100,000, and the highest death rate, 54 per 100,000.
Among American white men, the rate is about 135 per 100,000. There are about 89 cases per 100,000 among Hispanic and Japanese-American men; the rate is lower still for other Asian-Americans.
